etymology: From mighty, Saxon mihtig, and the adverbial -ly. Webster 1828: with great power, force, or vehemence; with strength. Scripture uses it of the Spirit falling on a man, of the word of God spreading, of a city crying to God, and of God working in a labouring apostle.
biblical_def: Mightily in Scripture describes power at work, and its subject is almost always God. Luke summarises the whole Ephesian ministry — the burned books, the failed exorcists, the riot of the silversmiths — in seven words: So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed (Acts 19:20). The word grows; the word prevails; the men are instruments. The same adverb marks the Spirit’s descent on Samson: the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and he rent him as he would have rent a kid, and he had nothing in his hand (Judges 14:6). Note the sequence Scripture insists on: the strength was the Spirit’s, not the man’s, and it came upon a man whose private life was already compromised. Paul describes his own labour the same way, refusing to separate his effort from God’s working: Whereunto I also labour, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily (Colossians 1:29) — genuine striving, genuinely his, and the energy in it God’s. And the king of Nineveh commands the word of a repenting city: let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way (Jonah 3:8).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MIGHTILY as with great power, force, or strength; vigorously; powerfully; with great earnestness or vehemence; and, in a secondary sense, greatly or to a great degree.
webster_full: MIGHTILY, adv. — With great power, force, or strength; vigorously; powerfully.
Vehemently; with great earnestness; as, to cry mightily unto God.
Greatly; to a great degree; very much; as, the word grew mightily.
In Scripture, most often of the operation of the Spirit of God upon men, or of the progress of His word.
From mighty, Saxon mihtig, from miht, might — the root also of may and main.
scriptures: Acts 19:20
So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed.
Judges 14:6
And the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and he rent him as he would have rent a kid, and he had nothing in his hand: but he told not his father or his mother what he had done.
Colossians 1:29
Whereunto I also labour, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily.
Jonah 3:8
But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands.
corruption_summary: Colossians 1:29 puts genuine human striving and God’s working in the same clause, which refutes both the quietist counsel to let go and let God and the activist assumption that ministry advances by human energy adequately applied.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul’s sentence is deliberately double: I also labour, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily. The labour is his, the striving is his — the word is agonizomenos, the language of the wrestling ring — and the energy that does the work is God’s. The Higher Life and Keswick tradition, with its counsel to cease from striving and let Christ live the life, has half the verse; the ministry-as-management approach, with its confidence that the right structures and sufficient effort produce growth, has the other half. Philippians 2:12-13 states the same doctrine in the same shape: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure. The for is the whole argument.

Judges 14:6 guards against a different error, the assumption that unusual power in a man’s ministry certifies his character. The Spirit came mightily on Samson while he was on his way to marry a Philistine woman against his parents’ counsel, and He came mightily on him again after worse. Gifts are given for the people, not as a testimonial to the man; Christ warned of those who would say have we not prophesied in thy name? and be told I never knew you. Acts 19:20 supplies the healthier measure. The thing Luke reports as growing mightily and prevailing is not a man’s influence but the word of God, and that is the only statistic the New Testament ever boasts in.
roots_summary: Greek ischuo (G2480), to be strong, to prevail; energeia (G1753), operative power, energy; dunamis (G1411), power; Hebrew tsalach (H6743), to rush upon, to prosper; chozqah (H2394), with force.
roots_lines: Greek ischuo (G2480) — to be strong, to prevail; so mightily grew the word of God and prevailed (Acts 19:20).
Greek energeia (G1753) — effectual working; his working, which worketh in me mightily (Colossians 1:29).
Greek agonizomai (G75) — to contend as in the games; the striving of the same verse.
Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to rush, to break out upon; the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him (Judges 14:6).
Hebrew chozqah (H2394) — strength, force; cry mightily unto God (Jonah 3:8).
usage: So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed (Acts 19:20) — the word grows, the men are instruments.
The Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him (Judges 14:6) — power given for the people, not as a testimonial to the man.
His working, which worketh in me mightily (Colossians 1:29) — real striving, and the energy in it God’s.

etymology: The comparative of mighty, Saxon mihtig. Webster 1828: having more power or strength; more forcible. In the Gospels it is John the Baptist’s word for the One coming after him, and it is the pivot of his whole message.
biblical_def: Mightier is a word of comparison, and Scripture uses it at the exact points where a comparison has to be made and got right. John the Baptist, at the height of his influence, with all Judaea coming out to him, makes the only comparison that matters: he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire (Matthew 3:11), and in Luke, one mightier than I cometh, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose (Luke 3:16). Unloosing a sandal was the work of a slave, and the greatest of those born of women says he is unfit for it. The psalmist makes the comparison against the sea, which for the Hebrew mind was the image of untameable chaos: The LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, yea, than the mighty waves of the sea (Psalm 93:4). And Pharaoh makes the comparison that begins the oppression and betrays its motive: Behold, the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we (Exodus 1:9) — fear of a growing people, which produced the midwives’ command and, in God’s providence, produced Moses.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives MIGHTIER as the comparative of MIGHTY: having more power, strength, or force; more able; more forcible or violent; greater in influence or effect.
webster_full: MIGHTIER, a. — The comparative of MIGHTY; having more power or strength than another.
MIGHTY, a. — Having great bodily strength or physical power; very strong or vigorous.
Very great in any respect; powerful in influence, in wealth, or in achievement.
Violent; vehement; as, a mighty wind, or waters mightier than the sea.
From Saxon mihtig, from miht, might — the root also of main, may, and dismay.
scriptures: Matthew 3:11
I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:
Luke 3:16

John answered, saying unto them all, I indeed baptize you with water; but one mightier than I cometh, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire:
Psalm 93:4
The LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, yea, than the mighty waves of the sea.
Exodus 1:9
And he said unto his people, Behold, the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we:
corruption_summary: John the Baptist’s ministry is the standing rebuke to platform-building, since he says mightier than I at the moment of his greatest influence and later adds that he must decrease.
corruption_paragraphs: John had a movement. Matthew says Jerusalem and all Judaea and all the region round about Jordan went out to him; Josephus records his fame independently; his disciples were still a distinct group decades later in Ephesus. At that moment he tells the crowds that the One coming after him is mightier and that he is not fit to carry His sandals. When his own disciples complain that everyone is going to Jesus instead, he answers He must increase, but I must decrease. The contemporary structure of Christian ministry — personal platforms, named conferences, followings attached to individuals — is not condemned in every instance by that example, but it is measured by it, and the measure is uncomfortable. The test John applies is not whether a man has influence but where he points it.

Psalm 93:4 supplies the theological ground for the comparison. In the ancient Near Eastern imagination the sea was chaos, the untameable enemy, and the surrounding nations told myths of a god who fought and subdued it. The psalm makes no such contest: the LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, and the psalm opens with The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty… the world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved. There is no battle because there is no rival. Exodus 1:9 shows the same doctrine from the underside: Pharaoh, the mightiest man on earth, is afraid of shepherds, and every measure he takes to contain them advances the deliverance he fears.
roots_summary: Greek ischuros (G2478), strong, mighty; ischuroteros, the comparative; Hebrew addir (H117), majestic, mighty; atsum (H6099), numerous, mighty.
roots_lines: Greek ischuroteros — the comparative of ischuros (G2478), strong; John’s word for the coming Christ (Matthew 3:11).
Greek himas (G2438) — a thong, a latchet; the sandal-strap John says he is unworthy to unloose (Luke 3:16).
Hebrew addir (H117) — majestic, glorious, mighty; the LORD on high is mightier (Psalm 93:4).
Hebrew atsum (H6099) — numerous, vast, mighty; Pharaoh’s description of Israel (Exodus 1:9).
Hebrew gibbor (H1368) — a mighty man, a champion; The mighty God of Isaiah 9:6.
usage: He that cometh after me is mightier than I (Matthew 3:11) — said at the height of John’s own influence.
The LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters (Psalm 93:4) — no contest, because no rival.
The children of Israel are more and mightier than we (Exodus 1:9) — the mightiest man on earth afraid of shepherds.

etymology: From valiant, Old French vaillant, from Latin valere, to be strong. Webster 1828: with personal strength or intrepidity; courageously. Scripture uses it only of doing, never of feeling — and always with God named as the one who makes it possible.
biblical_def: Valiantly occurs a handful of times in Scripture and the pattern is unvarying: the courage is commanded, the doing is the man’s, and the outcome is God’s. The psalm states it twice, word for word, in two different books: Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies (Psalm 60:12; Psalm 108:13). The valour is real and it is through God; the treading down is His alone. Balaam, forced to bless, uses the word of Israel’s future: And Edom shall be a possession, Seir also shall be a possession for his enemies; and Israel shall do valiantly (Numbers 24:18). And Joab, caught between the Syrians before him and the Ammonites behind, gives one of the finest speeches in Scripture and ends it with a submission that is the whole doctrine in a clause: Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight (1 Chronicles 19:13). He will fight as hard as he can, for the right things, and leave the result entirely with God — without knowing in advance whether the result will be victory.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines VALIANTLY as with personal strength and intrepidity; courageously; stoutly; bravely; with the vigour and resolution proper to a valiant man.
webster_full: VALIANTLY, adv. — With personal strength and intrepidity; courageously; stoutly; bravely.
VALIANT, a. — Brave; courageous; intrepid in danger; heroic.
Performed with valour; as, a valiant act or a valiant defence.
Applied in Scripture to men of war, and to those who behave themselves so for their people and their cities.
From Latin valeo, to be strong — the root also of value, valid, prevail, and convalesce.
scriptures: Psalm 60:12
Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies.
Psalm 108:13
Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies.
1 Chronicles 19:13
Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight.
Numbers 24:18
And Edom shall be a possession, Seir also shall be a possession for his enemies; and Israel shall do valiantly.
corruption_summary: Joab’s formula — fight as hard as you can and leave the outcome with the LORD — is refused by the prosperity teaching that guarantees the outcome in advance and by the fatalism that concludes effort is therefore pointless.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Chronicles 19:13 deserves to be memorised. Joab has divided his force, taken the harder half himself, given Abishai a plan for mutual rescue, and then says: Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight. Every element is there. The courage is commanded, not felt into existence. The object is other people and the cities of God, not personal glory. And the outcome is surrendered without a guarantee — he does not say the LORD will give victory, he says let the LORD do what is good. That last clause is the one the prosperity teaching cannot say, because it has promised the result, and it is the one fatalism refuses to earn, because it has declined the fight.

Psalm 60 is worth reading whole for the same reason. It opens with defeat: O God, thou hast cast us off, thou hast scattered us… thou hast made the earth to tremble, and it complains that God goes not out with their armies. Only after that does it reach Through God we shall do valiantly. The confidence is not the absence of the complaint but its resolution, and the psalm places the whole of the valour under the preposition: through God. Numbers 24:18 shows the same doctrine from an unexpected mouth — a hired diviner announcing that Israel shall do valiantly, because God had determined it and no fee could alter the oracle.
roots_summary: Hebrew chayil (H2428), strength, force, an army, valour; chazaq (H2388), to be strong; Greek andrizomai (G407), to act like a man, to be courageous; krataios (G2900), mighty.
roots_lines: Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, valour, an army, and also wealth; we shall do valiantly (Psalm 60:12).
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to strengthen oneself; be of good courage (1 Chronicles 19:13).
Hebrew gibbor chayil — a mighty man of valour; the standing title for Israel’s warriors, and of Gideon before he had done anything.
Greek andrizomai (G407) — to play the man, to be courageous; quit you like men, be strong (1 Corinthians 16:13).
Greek tharreo (G2292) — to be of good courage, to be confident (2 Corinthians 5:6).
usage: Through God we shall do valiantly (Psalm 60:12) — the valour real, and under a preposition.
Let us behave ourselves valiantly… and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight (1 Chronicles 19:13) — the whole doctrine in one sentence.
Israel shall do valiantly (Numbers 24:18) — announced by a diviner who was paid to say the opposite.

etymology: From stedfast (the Authorized Version’s spelling of steadfast), Saxon stedefaest — fixed in place, from stede, a place, and faest, fast. Webster 1828: with fixedness or firmness; with constancy or resolution.
biblical_def: Stedfastly means fixed in place, and Scripture uses it of the four things the church did, of the Lord’s face set toward Jerusalem, of a dying man’s gaze, and of a widow’s settled resolve. Of the first church: And they continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers (Acts 2:42). Four things, and nothing else is listed — the apostolic teaching, the common life, the Lord’s table, and prayer. Of the Lord: when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), which begins the long central section of Luke’s Gospel and describes a man walking deliberately toward His own execution. Of Stephen, in the moment of his death: being full of the Holy Ghost, looked up stedfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God (Acts 7:55) — and the Son of man is standing, not seated, to receive him. And of Ruth, whose fixedness ended an argument: When she saw that she was stedfastly minded to go with her, then she left speaking unto her (Ruth 1:18).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines STEDFASTLY as with fixedness or firmness; with constancy; with steadiness of mind or of the eye; resolutely and without wavering.
webster_full: STEDFASTLY, adv. — With fixedness or firmness; with constancy; resolutely.
With a fixed and unwavering gaze; as, to look stedfastly upon a thing.
STEDFAST, a. — Fast fixed; firm; not to be moved from its place or purpose.
Constant; resolute; not fickle or wavering; as, stedfast in the faith.
From Saxon stede, a place, and faest, fast — literally, fixed in place.
scriptures: Acts 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Luke 9:51
And it came to pass, when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem,
Acts 7:55
But he, being full of the Holy Ghost, looked up stedfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God,
Ruth 1:18
When she saw that she was stedfastly minded to go with her, then she left speaking unto her.
corruption_summary: Acts 2:42 lists exactly four things the first church continued stedfastly in, and the modern congregation that has added a great deal to that list while quietly subtracting from it should notice which of the four is usually the first to go.
corruption_paragraphs: The four are the apostles’ doctrine, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayers. That is the whole inventory. It is worth asking any congregation which of the four its calendar actually protects. Doctrine is often reduced to a doctrinal statement nobody reads and a preaching diet that avoids the harder texts. Fellowship becomes attendance. The breaking of bread — whether one reads it of the Lord’s Supper, the common meal, or both together — is frequently quarterly. And the prayer meeting is, in most churches, the least attended gathering of the week, which is a plain statement about what the congregation believes accomplishes anything. The regulative principle is not a fussy restriction; it is the instinct that what God appointed is sufficient and that additions crowd out the appointed things.

Luke 9:51 sets the word in its most solemn use. Christ stedfastly set his face toward Jerusalem when the time came — a Hebrew idiom for immovable resolve, borrowed from Isaiah 50:7, therefore have I set my face like a flint. He was not swept along by events, arrested by surprise, or overtaken by a plot. He walked toward the cross deliberately, at the hour appointed, having told His disciples three times what waited there. Acts 7:55 shows the fruit of the same steadiness in a man about to be stoned: full of the Holy Ghost, looking stedfastly into heaven, seeing Jesus standing. That is what fixedness produces at the end, and it is why Paul urges the Corinthians to be stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord.
roots_summary: Greek proskartereo (G4342), to continue steadfastly, to persist in; atenizo (G816), to fix the eyes upon, to gaze intently; sterizo (G4741), to fix, to establish; Hebrew amets (H553), to be firm.
roots_lines: Greek proskartereo (G4342) — to attend constantly, to persevere in; they continued stedfastly (Acts 2:42).
Greek atenizo (G816) — to gaze fixedly; Stephen looked up stedfastly into heaven (Acts 7:55).
Greek sterizo (G4741) — to set fast, to establish; he stedfastly set his face (Luke 9:51).
Greek hedraios (G1476) — seated, settled, steadfast; be ye stedfast, unmoveable (1 Corinthians 15:58).
Hebrew amets (H553) — to be alert, firm, determined; she was stedfastly minded (Ruth 1:18).
usage: They continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine (Acts 2:42) — four things, and no others listed.
He stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51) — a man walking deliberately toward His own execution.
Looked up stedfastly into heaven… and Jesus standing (Acts 7:55) — and He is standing, not seated, to receive him.

etymology: From withstand, Saxon withstandan — with in its older sense of against, and stand. Webster 1828: opposed; resisted, either with physical or moral means. Literally, to stand against.
biblical_def: Withstood means stood against, and Scripture gives four instances that between them cover almost every legitimate and illegitimate form of resistance. Paul withstood an apostle publicly and gives his reason in the same breath: But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed (Galatians 2:11) — not for a doctrinal statement Peter had made but for a table he had withdrawn from, because the gospel was at stake in the practice. Priests withstood a king who had taken a censer into the temple: they withstood Uzziah the king, and said unto him, It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests (2 Chronicles 26:18), and God struck him with leprosy on the spot. An angel reports being withstood in the unseen realm: the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me (Daniel 10:13) — three weeks of Daniel’s praying while an answer was delayed by a conflict he could not see. And Paul names the pattern of resistance to truth itself: as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth: men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith (2 Timothy 3:8).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WITHSTOOD as the past tense and participle of WITHSTAND: opposed; resisted; stood against, either by physical force or by argument and remonstrance.
webster_full: WITHSTOOD, pret. and pp. of WITHSTAND — Opposed; resisted; stood in opposition to.
WITHSTAND, v.t. — To oppose; to resist, either with physical or moral force.
To stand against; to hold out against; as, to withstand an assault or a temptation.
To resist by argument, remonstrance, or open rebuke, as one man withstanding another to the face.
From with, in the old sense of against, and stand; compare withhold and withdraw.
scriptures: Galatians 2:11
But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.
2 Chronicles 26:18

And they withstood Uzziah the king, and said unto him, It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated to burn incense: go out of the sanctuary; for thou hast trespassed; neither shall it be for thine honour from the LORD God.
Daniel 10:13
But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me; and I remained there with the kings of Persia.
2 Timothy 3:8
Now as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth: men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith.
corruption_summary: Galatians 2:11 records one apostle publicly rebuking another over conduct, and both the deference that will not confront a leader and the online habit of confronting everyone about everything mistake what Paul actually did.
corruption_paragraphs: The circumstances are worth noting because they bound the example. Peter had eaten with Gentiles and then withdrew when men came from James, and other Jews and even Barnabas were carried away with his dissimulation. Paul’s charge is that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel. So the rebuke was public because the sin was public and its effect was spreading; it was over an action, not a suspicion; it concerned the gospel itself, not a preference; and it was delivered face to face by a man of equal standing. Every one of those features is usually missing from the modern confrontation, which is typically about an inference, delivered to an audience rather than a face, and concerning a matter of taste. Matthew 18 governs private offences; Galatians 2 governs public ones. Neither authorises what social media has made ordinary.

2 Chronicles 26:18 and Daniel 10:13 show two other kinds. Azariah and eighty priests withstood a king at the height of his success — Uzziah had built towers, dug wells, and made engines of war, and Scripture says when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction. Withstanding him was dangerous, and they did it anyway, on the ground of what appertained to whom. Daniel’s case is the one that should shape a believer’s prayers: he had been fasting three weeks with no answer, and the angel says the answer left on the first day and was withstood. Delay is not always refusal, and what delays it may be nothing the praying man could have known about.
roots_summary: Greek anthistemi (G436), to set oneself against, to withstand; Hebrew amad al, to stand against; Greek antitasso (G498), to arrange in battle against; histemi (G2476), to stand.
roots_lines: Greek anthistemi (G436) — to stand against, to resist; I withstood him to the face (Galatians 2:11) and Resist the devil (James 4:7).
Greek antitasso (G498) — to set in battle array against; God resisteth the proud (James 4:6).
Greek histemi (G2476) — to stand; the root of the whole family, and of having done all, to stand (Ephesians 6:13).
Hebrew amad (H5975) — to stand, to take a stand; the priests standing against Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:18).
Aramaic sar — prince; the prince of the kingdom of Persia (Daniel 10:13), a spiritual power over a nation.
usage: I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed (Galatians 2:11) — public sin, public rebuke, equal standing.
They withstood Uzziah the king (2 Chronicles 26:18) — eighty priests against a king at the height of his success.
The prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days (Daniel 10:13) — delay is not always refusal.

etymology: The comparative of strong, Saxon strang. Webster 1828: having more strength or power. Scripture uses it in comparisons that overturn the expected order — the weakness of God stronger than men, a prophet overpowered by the God he served.
biblical_def: Stronger in Scripture is nearly always used to overturn an expectation. Paul’s statement is the boldest: Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men (1 Corinthians 1:25). There is no foolishness in God and no weakness in Him; Paul is speaking of the cross as the world judges it, and saying that what men take for God’s weakest act outmatches their strongest. Jeremiah uses the word in a complaint that is also a confession: O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me (Jeremiah 20:7). He had resolved to stop preaching, and could not, because the word was as a burning fire shut up in my bones. Christ uses it of Himself in the parable of the strong man: when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils (Luke 11:22). And the chronicler measures a long conflict in one sentence: David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker (2 Samuel 3:1).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives STRONGER as the comparative of STRONG: having more physical or moral power; more able to sustain or resist; more forcible or cogent, as an argument.
webster_full: STRONGER, a. — The comparative of STRONG; having greater power or force than another.
STRONG, a. — Having physical active power, or great power of acting; vigorous; able to sustain or resist.
Having moral or intellectual force; cogent; as, a strong argument or a strong reason.
Fortified; able to resist attack; as, a strong city or a strong hold.
From Saxon strang, strong — the root also of strength, string, and strain.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 1:25
Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
Jeremiah 20:7
O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me.
Luke 11:22
But when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils.
2 Samuel 3:1
Now there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker.
corruption_summary: Luke 11:22 pictures Satan as a strong man already overcome, disarmed and plundered by a stronger, which contradicts the popular Christianity that treats the devil as an active rival whose defeat still hangs on the believer’s technique.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable is the Lord’s own answer to the charge that He cast out devils by Beelzebub. A strong man armed keeps his palace and his goods are in peace — that is the world under the god of this world — but when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils. Each exorcism is a piece of plunder carried out of a house already entered. Colossians 2:15 says Christ spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it — at the cross, in the past tense. The believer’s warfare is real and Ephesians 6 arms him for it, but he fights from a victory, not toward one, and Scripture nowhere makes the outcome depend on the right formula spoken with sufficient authority.

Jeremiah 20:7 is worth defending because it embarrasses modern readers in both directions. The prophet says God deceived him — the Hebrew is a strong word, used elsewhere of enticing — and says that God was stronger and prevailed. He is not accusing God of falsehood; he is saying he was overpowered into an office that has cost him everything and that he cannot lay down. Scripture records the complaint without correcting it, and two verses later Jeremiah says he resolved to speak no more in God’s name and found he could not forbear. A canon that includes this is a canon that does not require the sufferer to be composed, and 1 Corinthians 1:25 explains why the whole pattern holds: God’s apparent weakness is stronger than men’s strength.
roots_summary: Greek ischuros (G2478), strong; ischuroteros, stronger; asthenes (G772), weak; Hebrew chazaq (H2388), strong, firm; pathah (H6601), to entice, to persuade.
roots_lines: Greek ischuroteros — comparative of ischuros (G2478); the weakness of God is stronger than men (1 Corinthians 1:25).
Greek asthenes (G772) — without strength, weak; the term Paul deliberately applies to God’s act at the cross as men judge it.
Greek panoplia (G3833) — full armour; the strong man’s armour taken in Luke 11:22, and the believer’s in Ephesians 6:11.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to prevail; thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed (Jeremiah 20:7).
Hebrew pathah (H6601) — to entice, to persuade, to open; the verb the KJV renders deceived in the same verse.
usage: The weakness of God is stronger than men (1 Corinthians 1:25) — the cross as the world judges it, outmatching man’s best.
Thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed (Jeremiah 20:7) — a prophet overpowered into an office he cannot lay down.
When a stronger than he shall come upon him (Luke 11:22) — the strong man already entered, disarmed, and plundered.

etymology: From Latin constringere, to bind together, from con and stringere, to draw tight. Webster 1828: compelled; forced; urged with irresistible power. The root image is a binding that leaves no other course open.
biblical_def: Constrained in Scripture describes a pressure that leaves no other course open, and it comes from love as often as from necessity. Two of the loveliest instances are hospitality that would not take no for an answer. The disciples at Emmaus, walking with a stranger who made as though He would go further: But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them (Luke 24:29) — and it was in the breaking of bread that they knew Him. Lydia, newly baptized at Philippi, does the same to Paul’s company: If ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and abide there. And she constrained us (Acts 16:15). The word is also used of the Lord’s own hand on His disciples: straightway Jesus constrained his disciples to get into a ship, and to go before him unto the other side (Matthew 14:22) — He sent them deliberately into the storm that followed. And Paul uses it of a legal necessity forced on him by opposition: when the Jews spake against it, I was constrained to appeal unto Caesar; not that I had ought to accuse my nation of (Acts 28:19).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CONSTRAINED as urged with irresistible power or by strong motives; compelled; forced; restrained or confined; also, produced by compulsion and therefore not free or natural.
webster_full: CONSTRAINED, pp. — Urged with irresistible power or by strong motives; compelled; forced.
Restrained; confined; held back from acting freely.
Produced by compulsion; not voluntary; as, a constrained manner or a constrained assent.
In Scripture, used both of pressing hospitality upon a guest and of a necessity laid on a man by circumstances or by God.
From Latin con and stringo, to draw tight — the root also of strain, restrain, and stringent.
scriptures: Luke 24:29
But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them.
Acts 16:15
And when she was baptized, and her household, she besought us, saying, If ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and abide there. And she constrained us.
Matthew 14:22
And straightway Jesus constrained his disciples to get into a ship, and to go before him unto the other side, while he sent the multitudes away.
Acts 28:19
But when the Jews spake against it, I was constrained to appeal unto Caesar; not that I had ought to accuse my nation of.
corruption_summary: Matthew 14:22 has Christ deliberately putting His disciples into the boat that ran into the storm, which contradicts the widespread assumption that obedience to God’s leading is confirmed by calm conditions.
corruption_paragraphs: The chronology is exact and worth stating plainly. Jesus constrained His disciples to get into the ship; He sent the multitudes away; He went up into a mountain to pray; and the ship was in the midst of the sea, tossed with waves, the wind contrary. They were in the storm because He put them there, and He was praying while they laboured. Against the common test — that a door which opens smoothly is God’s will and difficulty means a wrong turn — this narrative sets a storm entered by direct command. Paul was shipwrecked on the way to a destination God had promised him. The dictionary holds that circumstances are providence and providence is not self-interpreting; the will of God is known from His revealed word, and the road it puts a man on may be rough for reasons he learns later or never.

The two hospitality texts are the happier use and they are worth pressing on modern habits. The Emmaus disciples constrained a stranger to stay, and received the risen Christ at their table. Lydia argued the apostles into her house on the ground of her own new baptism — if ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord — which is a remarkable piece of reasoning from a woman converted that morning. Hebrews 13:2 says some have entertained angels unawares, and 1 Peter 4:9 commands hospitality without grudging. In an age where households are private and invitations are rare, this pressing, insistent, slightly inconvenient hospitality is a New Testament practice the church has quietly dropped.
roots_summary: Greek parabiazomai (G3849), to constrain by entreaty, to urge strongly; anagkazo (G315), to compel, to necessitate; sunecho (G4912), to hold together, to press; Hebrew patsar (H6484), to urge, to press.
roots_lines: Greek parabiazomai (G3849) — to use force upon by entreaty; used only of the Emmaus disciples and of Lydia (Luke 24:29; Acts 16:15).
Greek anagkazo (G315) — to compel, to necessitate; Jesus constrained his disciples (Matthew 14:22) and Paul’s appeal to Caesar (Acts 28:19).
Greek sunecho (G4912) — to hold together, to press upon; the love of Christ constraineth us (2 Corinthians 5:14).
Hebrew patsar (H6484) — to press, to urge; used of Lot pressing the angels to turn in to his house (Genesis 19:3).
Greek ananke (G318) — necessity; necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:16).
usage: They constrained him, saying, Abide with us (Luke 24:29) — insistent hospitality, and the risen Christ at the table.
And she constrained us (Acts 16:15) — a woman converted that morning arguing apostles into her house.
Jesus constrained his disciples to get into a ship (Matthew 14:22) — sent by command into the storm that followed.

etymology: From Latin urgere, to press, to drive, to push. Webster 1828: pressed; incited; importuned; provoked. Scripture uses it of pressing a gift on a reluctant man, of pressing a secret out of a strong one, and of pressing a prophet against his better judgment.
biblical_def: Urged in Scripture describes persistent pressure, and the four instances form an instructive set. Jacob urges a gift on Esau after twenty years of fear, and the reconciliation is sealed by the taking of it: Take, I pray thee, my blessing that is brought to thee; because God hath dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough. And he urged him, and he took it (Genesis 33:11). Elisha refuses payment from a healed Syrian general, and holds firm under exactly the same pressure: As the LORD liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none. And he urged him to take it; but he refused (2 Kings 5:16) — the refusal that Gehazi would undo within the hour, to his ruin. The sons of the prophets press Elisha to send a search party for Elijah when he has told them not to: when they urged him till he was ashamed, he said, Send (2 Kings 2:17) — a man of God worn down into conceding what he knew was pointless. And Delilah’s method is described with the same verb: when she pressed him daily with her words, and urged him, so that his soul was vexed unto death (Judges 16:16).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines URGED as pressed; driven; incited; importuned; pressed with argument or entreaty; provoked or stimulated to action.
webster_full: URGED, pp. — Pressed; driven; incited; impelled with earnestness.
Importuned; solicited with earnestness and repetition.
Pressed with argument or with entreaty; as, he urged him to take the gift.
Provoked; stimulated; as, urged to anger by continual reproach.
From Latin urgeo, to press — the root also of urgent and, remotely, of wreak.
scriptures: Genesis 33:11
Take, I pray thee, my blessing that is brought to thee; because God hath dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough. And he urged him, and he took it.
2 Kings 5:16
But he said, As the LORD liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none. And he urged him to take it; but he refused.
2 Kings 2:17
And when they urged him till he was ashamed, he said, Send. They sent therefore fifty men; and they sought three days, but found him not.
Judges 16:16
And it came to pass, when she pressed him daily with her words, and urged him, so that his soul was vexed unto death;
corruption_summary: Elisha refused Naaman’s payment under heavy pressure and Gehazi took it in secret an hour later, which is the Bible’s plainest case study in the commercialising of ministry.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter sets the two men side by side deliberately. Elisha, urged by a grateful and very rich foreigner, swears he will receive none, and the reason is theological rather than ascetic: the healing was God’s and could not be sold without misrepresenting Him. Gehazi’s reasoning is the reasoning of every commercialised ministry since: my master hath spared Naaman this Syrian, in not receiving at his hands that which he brought: but, as the LORD liveth, I will run after him, and take somewhat of him. He swears by the LORD while planning the theft. The leprosy that leaves Naaman fastens on Gehazi, which Scripture reports without comment. Peter states the standard for elders directly: feed the flock not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind (1 Peter 5:2).

The two remaining instances warn in different directions. 2 Kings 2:17 records Elisha, who knew Elijah was gone, conceding a three-day search because fifty men urged him till he was ashamed. Shame is an effective lever against a leader, and men who cannot be argued out of a position can often be embarrassed out of it. Judges 16:16 shows the same pressure applied to Samson by a woman paid to find his secret, daily, until his soul was vexed unto death — and he told her. Against these, Genesis 33:11 shows urging at its best: Jacob pressing a gift on the brother he had wronged, and the taking of it being the sign that the wrong was covered.
roots_summary: Hebrew patsar (H6484), to press, to urge; alats (H509), to press, to urge; uts (H213), to press, to hasten; Greek parabiazomai (G3849), to constrain by entreaty.
roots_lines: Hebrew patsar (H6484) — to press, to push, to urge; he urged him, and he took it (Genesis 33:11) and he urged him to take it (2 Kings 5:16).
Hebrew alats (H509) — to press, to urge; she pressed him daily with her words, and urged him (Judges 16:16).
Hebrew uts (H213) — to press, to be narrow, to hasten; the sense of crowding a man toward a decision.
Hebrew bosh (H954) — to be ashamed; when they urged him till he was ashamed (2 Kings 2:17).
Greek parabiazomai (G3849) — the New Testament equivalent, to constrain by entreaty (Luke 24:29).
usage: He urged him, and he took it (Genesis 33:11) — a gift pressed on a wronged brother, and taken.
He urged him to take it; but he refused (2 Kings 5:16) — the healing was God’s and could not be sold.
When they urged him till he was ashamed (2 Kings 2:17) — shame as a lever against a man who could not be argued.

etymology: From Latin patiens, the present participle of pati, to suffer, to endure. Webster 1828: having the quality of enduring evils without murmuring; not easily provoked; calmly waiting for something expected. The word means suffering before it means waiting.
biblical_def: Patient in the New Testament is a duty of every believer, a qualification for office, and a description of the farmer who has no other option. Paul lists it in his short catalogue of how a congregation deals with its own difficult members: warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men (1 Thessalonians 5:14). Four different responses to four different people — the unruly are warned, the fainthearted comforted, the weak supported — and patience covers them all. It is required in an elder: the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient (2 Timothy 2:24), and the context is a man dealing with people who oppose themselves. James grounds the church’s patience in an event: Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain (James 5:7) — the farmer’s patience is not resignation but confidence in a harvest he cannot hurry. And the Preacher weighs it against its opposite: Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit (Ecclesiastes 7:8).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PATIENT as having the quality of enduring evils without murmuring or fretfulness; sustaining afflictions with fortitude and submission to the divine will; not easily provoked; calmly waiting for what is expected.
webster_full: PATIENT, a. — Having the quality of enduring evils without murmuring or fretfulness.
Sustaining afflictions of body or mind with fortitude, calmness, or Christian submission to the divine will.
Not easily provoked; calm under the sufferance of injuries or offences.
Persevering; constant in pursuit or exertion; calmly diligent; and, waiting with calmness or contentment.
From Latin patior, to suffer — the root also of passion, compassion, and passive.
scriptures: 1 Thessalonians 5:14
Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men.
2 Timothy 2:24
And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,
James 5:7

Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain.
Ecclesiastes 7:8
Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.
corruption_summary: 1 Thessalonians 5:14 assigns four different treatments to four different kinds of people, and the modern pastoral instinct that applies comfort universally gives the unruly exactly what Paul says not to give them.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul’s verse is a piece of pastoral triage and the distinctions are the point. Warn them that are unruly — the word is military, of a soldier out of rank; such a man needs admonition, not sympathy. Comfort the feebleminded — literally the small-souled, the discouraged; they need consolation, not warning. Support the weak — hold them up, which implies a burden actually carried. And then, over all three, be patient toward all men. A ministry that comforts everyone will confirm the unruly in their disorder; a ministry that warns everyone will crush the fainthearted. Getting the category wrong is not a small mistake, and the same apostle who wrote this wrote that the servant of the Lord must be apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves.

James 5:7 sets the whole matter in the only frame that makes it bearable. The farmer waits because the harvest is certain and the rains are appointed, not because waiting is a virtue in itself. Christian patience is eschatological: be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord, and James adds two verses later, the coming of the Lord draweth nigh… behold, the judge standeth before the door. Where the second coming becomes a distant abstraction, patience loses its object and turns into mere endurance or, more often, into demands for immediate resolution. Ecclesiastes 7:8 states the alternative bluntly: the patient in spirit is better than the proud, and pride is the reason most impatience exists.
roots_summary: Greek makrothumeo (G3114), to be long-tempered, to be patient; makrothumia (G3115), longsuffering; hupomone (G5281), endurance under a load; anexikakos (G420), patient of wrong.
roots_lines: Greek makrothumeo (G3114) — to be long-tempered, slow to anger; be patient toward all men (1 Thessalonians 5:14) and the farmer of James 5:7.
Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering; a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22) and an attribute of God (Romans 2:4).
Greek hupomone (G5281) — endurance, remaining under a weight; the patience that worketh experience (Romans 5:3).
Greek anexikakos (G420) — enduring evil without resentment; the patient of 2 Timothy 2:24.
Greek ataktos (G813) — disorderly, out of rank; the unruly of 1 Thessalonians 5:14, a military term.
usage: Warn them that are unruly… be patient toward all men (1 Thessalonians 5:14) — four treatments, four kinds of people.
Apt to teach, patient (2 Timothy 2:24) — required of the man who must instruct those that oppose themselves.
The husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth (James 5:7) — patience with an object, not resignation.

etymology: From assured, Old French asseurer, from Latin ad and securus, secure. Webster 1828: certainly; indubitably; without doubt. In Acts it introduces the conclusion of the first Christian sermon, and in Jeremiah it describes how God intends to plant His people.
biblical_def: Assuredly in Scripture marks a certainty that may be acted upon, and its greatest use closes the sermon at Pentecost: Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made that same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36). Peter does not ask for consideration; he demands certain knowledge of two facts joined in one sentence — that God has made Him Lord and Christ, and that this same Jesus is the one they crucified. Three thousand were pricked in their heart at it. Luke uses the word again of how Paul’s company read a vision: after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them (Acts 16:10) — a conclusion drawn, not a feeling followed. God uses it of His own settled purpose toward a restored people: I will rejoice over them to do them good, and I will plant them in this land assuredly with my whole heart and with my whole soul (Jeremiah 32:41). And Nathan puts it in Bathsheba’s mouth to hold David to an oath: Assuredly Solomon thy son shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne (1 Kings 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ASSUREDLY as certainly; indubitably; without doubt or question; with entire confidence in the truth of what is affirmed.
webster_full: ASSUREDLY, adv. — Certainly; indubitably; without doubt.
With full confidence or entire persuasion of the truth of a thing.
ASSURED, a. — Certain; indubitable; not doubting; bold to excess in some uses.
In theology, assurance is the settled persuasion of one’s own interest in Christ, grounded on the promises and the witness of the Spirit.
From Latin ad and securus, secure — the root also of sure, secure, and insurance.
scriptures: Acts 2:36
Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made that same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ.
Acts 16:10
And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them.
Jeremiah 32:41
Yea, I will rejoice over them to do them good, and I will plant them in this land assuredly with my whole heart and with my whole soul.
1 Kings 1:13

Go and get thee in unto king David, and say unto him, Didst not thou, my lord, O king, swear unto thine handmaid, saying, Assuredly Solomon thy son shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne? why then doth Adonijah reign?
corruption_summary: Acts 2:36 makes certain knowledge the aim of preaching, which the modern preference for tentative, exploratory religious language treats as arrogance rather than as the apostolic pattern.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter’s conclusion is the model, and every feature of it is now unfashionable. He addresses a specific audience — all the house of Israel. He demands certainty — know assuredly. He states a fact about a Person, publicly verifiable in its historical part. And he names his hearers’ own guilt without softening: whom ye have crucified. The response was not offence but conviction; they were pricked in their heart and asked what they should do. Preaching that offers perspectives, journeys, and invitations to explore has abandoned the form the apostles used. The dictionary does not confuse this certainty with the preacher’s self-confidence; the certainty is about Christ, and it is held by men who elsewhere describe themselves as the chief of sinners and as earthen vessels.

Jeremiah 32:41 shows the ground on which such certainty rests, and it is not the strength of anyone’s conviction. God says He will plant His people in the land assuredly with my whole heart and with my whole soul — an extraordinary anthropomorphism for the wholeheartedness of divine purpose, spoken to a prophet who had just bought a field in a country about to be destroyed. The chapter is the great biblical picture of faith acting on a promise against every visible fact: Jeremiah paid seventeen shekels for land under Babylonian occupation, weighed the money, signed the deed, and had it sealed in an earthen vessel that they may continue many days. Assurance of that kind is not a temperament; it is a conclusion drawn from what God has said.
roots_summary: Greek asphalos (G806), safely, certainly; sumbibazo (G4822), to knit together, to conclude; plerophoria (G4136), full assurance; Hebrew emeth (H571), truth, faithfulness.
roots_lines: Greek asphalos (G806) — safely, assuredly, beyond slipping; let all the house of Israel know assuredly (Acts 2:36).
Greek sumbibazo (G4822) — to knit together, and so to conclude by reasoning; assuredly gathering (Acts 16:10).
Greek plerophoria (G4136) — full assurance; the full assurance of understanding (Colossians 2:2) and of faith (Hebrews 10:22).
Hebrew emeth (H571) — truth, firmness, faithfulness; from aman, to be firm, the root of amen.
Hebrew omnam (H551) — verily, truly; the assuredly of 1 Kings 1:13.
usage: Let all the house of Israel know assuredly (Acts 2:36) — certain knowledge demanded, and three thousand pricked in heart.
Assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us (Acts 16:10) — a conclusion drawn, not a feeling followed.
I will plant them in this land assuredly with my whole heart (Jeremiah 32:41) — said to a man buying a field under occupation.
